oneLine: Measure LLM speed as TTFT plus per-user TPS, report percentiles instead of the mean, and keep inference-only and end-to-end numbers apart so you know which layer to fix.
summary:
Two numbers describe how fast a streamed reply feels. **TTFT** is the wait before anything appears; prefill, which is compute-bound, accounts for most of it. **TPS** is the rate at which the rest arrives; decode sets it, and memory bandwidth limits decode. TPS is ambiguous: per user it is a latency number, summed across the service it is throughput. Say *perceived TPS* or *total TPS*, or quote **inter-token latency** (ITL): 10 ms between tokens is 100 tokens per second. Agents don't stream tool calls, so judge those by total response time.

Response times are right-skewed, so the mean drifts above the median and hides the slow tail. Report P50 for the typical request and P90, P95 or P99 for the tail, because users remember the one slow reply in ten (see 1.4.1).

Finally, decide what you are timing. Inference-only time is GPU work and shows whether model optimisation paid off. End-to-end time adds network and queueing and shows what users feel. Fast inference with slow end-to-end numbers means the problem is infrastructure (see 1.4.2).

mechanism.title: Prefill sets TTFT
mechanism.body: The model reads the whole prompt in one compute-heavy pass before it emits the first token.

mechanism.title: Decode sets TPS
mechanism.body: Each later token waits on a memory-bound step; its spacing is the inter-token latency.

mechanism.title: Collect a distribution
mechanism.body: Time many requests, sort them, and read P50 for the typical case and P90 or P99 for the tail.

mechanism.title: Split the clock
mechanism.body: Compare GPU-only time with client-side time; the gap is network plus queue.

callout.name: Fast GPU, slow app
callout.body: If inference-only numbers look healthy while users still wait, a faster kernel won't help. The missing time goes to the network, the request queue or too few replicas. Look at infrastructure first (see 1.4.2).

figureRefs.lookFor: The gap before the first token is TTFT; the steady spacing of the tokens after it is what TPS measures.
The long right tail drags the mean to the right of the P50 line.

keyCards.label: TTFT
keyCards.title: Wait before the first token
keyCards.body: Driven by prefill. Lower is better. Long prompts and queueing push it up.

keyCards.label: TPS / ITL
keyCards.title: Speed of the stream
keyCards.body: Driven by decode. TPS = 1000 / ITL in ms. Say perceived or total to avoid confusion.

keyCards.label: Percentiles
keyCards.title: P50 for typical, P99 for tail
keyCards.body: P90 means one request in ten is slower. The mean hides that tail.

keyCards.label: Scope
keyCards.title: Inference-only or end-to-end
keyCards.body: GPU time judges model work; client-side time judges what users feel.

workedExample.title: Mean versus percentiles on ten TTFT samples
workedExample.setup: A load test records the TTFT of ten requests, sorted: 150, 160, 165, 170, 175, 180, 190, 210, 650 and 1900 ms. Two requests hit a queue; the other eight were fine. Use the nearest-rank method: for percentile p over n samples, take the value at rank ceil(p × n / 100).

conclusion.text: The mean of 395 ms is more than double the median and matches no real request. P50 says the typical user waits 175 ms; P90 says one in ten waits at least 650 ms. Put those two on the dashboard and drop the mean.

checkQuestion.prompt: A streamed reply has a TTFT of 400 ms and 201 output tokens. After the first token, the remaining 200 tokens arrive at a steady 40 tokens per second. What is the total response time, from request to last token?
checkQuestion.methodHint: Total time is the wait for the first token plus the time to stream the tokens after it.
checkQuestion.workedSolution: Streaming the 200 tokens after the first takes 200 / 40 = 5 s = 5000 ms. Add the 400 ms TTFT: 400 + 5000 = 5400 ms.
checkQuestion.explanation: TTFT covers the first token, and TPS covers only the tokens after it, so total time is TTFT + (tokens after the first) / TPS. Dividing all 201 tokens by 40 gives 5025 ms and double-counts the first token.
checkQuestion.sourceQuote: How many tokens each second does the user receive after the first token is generated?

reflect.prompt: Your product manager asks why the latency dashboard shows P50 and P99 instead of one average, and why it has both a GPU timing panel and a client-side panel. Explain both choices in plain terms.
reflect.modelAnswer:
Response times for an LLM service are right-skewed: most requests cluster near a typical value, but a few take far longer because of long prompts, long outputs or a busy queue. An average mixes those together and lands somewhere that describes almost nobody, above the median. P50 tells us what the typical user gets. P99 tells us how bad the slow tail is, and users lose trust in the tail: if one reply in a hundred stalls for ten seconds, heavy users hit it every day. We track both and work to pull the tail down as well as the middle.

The two timing panels answer different questions. The GPU panel is inference-only time. It tells us whether model work, such as a new kernel or quantisation, made generation faster. The client-side panel is end-to-end time, including network and time waiting in the queue, and that is what users feel. When the GPU panel looks good but the client panel looks bad, the fix is infrastructure: more replicas, better autoscaling or a closer region.
points: LLM latency is right-skewed, so the mean sits above the median and describes few real requests.
P50 shows the typical experience; P90 or P99 shows the tail users remember.
Inference-only time measures whether model optimisation worked.
End-to-end time adds network and queueing and reflects what users feel.
Fast inference with slow end-to-end time points to infrastructure.

subsectionCards.hook: On skewed timings the mean misleads; read P50 through P99 instead.

subsectionCards.title: End-to-End Metrics
subsectionCards.hook: GPU time against the user's wait, and the gap that points to infrastructure.
